facts.claim: codex-cli 0.153.4 is installed at /usr/local/bin/codex on sail-gpu
facts.quote:
/usr/local/bin/codex
codex-cli 0.153.4
facts.notes: Source-code facts below were read at git tag rust-v0.153.4 of openai/codex (tag exists, sha 042fb41b7c813ac7999105e886b2b7aa715b5081), so they match the installed binary. A newer CLI exists (issue #46804 was filed against codex-cli 0.155.1); re-check flags after any upgrade.

facts.claim: codex exec -s/--sandbox accepts read-only, workspace-write, danger-full-access
facts.quote: -s, --sandbox <SANDBOX_MODE>  Select the sandbox policy to use when executing model-generated shell commands  [possible values: read-only, workspace-write, danger-full-access]
facts.notes: Not accepted by 'codex exec resume' (its --help has no -s, -C, --add-dir, --approve-for-me or -p).

facts.claim: codex exec defaults to a read-only sandbox
facts.quote: By default, `codex exec` runs in a read-only sandbox.
facts.notes: All developers.openai.com/codex/* doc URLs now 308-redirect to learn.chatgpt.com/docs/*. The same page gives: 'Allow edits: codex exec --sandbox workspace-write' and 'Allow broader access: codex exec --sandbox danger-full-access'.

facts.claim: In exec (headless) mode the approval policy defaults to 'never'. It switches to the config's policy only when the resolved reviewer is auto_review
facts.notes: The docs do not state this: the non-interactive page 'doesn't explicitly specify a default approval policy'. The evidence is the source code only; the exec tests (codex-rs/exec/tests/suite/approval_policy.rs) assert 'approval: on-request' when approvals_reviewer=auto_review.

facts.claim: Under exec's default 'never' approvals, a command that needs network or writes outside the writable roots is not escalated and does not wait. It fails inside the sandbox and the failure goes back to the model. Execpolicy 'prompt' rules become hard rejections
facts.quote: never:      Never ask for user approval Execution failures are immediately returned to the model  |  AskForApproval::Never => Some(PROMPT_CONFLICT_REASON),
facts.notes: Not tested at runtime on sail-gpu (running codex exec was outside the allowed command list).

facts.claim: approval_policy values are on-request, never and granular. 'untrusted' is retired
facts.quote: Controls when Codex pauses for approval before executing commands. You can also use `approval_policy = { granular = { ... } }` to allow or auto-reject specific prompt categories while keeping other prompts interactive.  |  Codex and ChatGPT Work no longer support `approval_policy = "untrusted"`
facts.notes: The top-level 'codex --help' -a lists only on-request and never. Granular keys per the config reference: sandbox_approval, rules, mcp_elicitations, request_permissions, skill_approval.

facts.claim: codex exec has no -a/--ask-for-approval flag, so its approval policy must be set with -c approval_policy=... (or --approve-for-me)
facts.quote: (codex --help only) -a, --ask-for-approval <APPROVAL_POLICY>  Configure when the model requires human approval before executing a command
facts.notes: The exec help also has no --search flag (the top-level one does) and no --full-auto.

facts.claim: --profile selects a named, deny-by-default permission profile
facts.quote: -p, --profile <CONFIG_PROFILE_V2>  Layer $CODEX_HOME/<name>.config.toml on top of the base user config
facts.notes: In 0.153.4, -p/--profile layers a config file ($CODEX_HOME/<name>.config.toml). It is not a permission profile. It is still useful for a per-role file such as builder.config.toml. Permission profiles are a separate mechanism (codex-09..11).

facts.claim: Named permission profiles exist: [permissions.<name>] tables selected with default_permissions. Built-ins are :read-only, :workspace, :danger-full-access. A custom profile with no filesystem entries stays restricted (deny-by-default). 'extends' inherits a built-in
facts.quote: Create a named profile under `[permissions.<name>]`, then set the top-level `default_permissions` key to that profile name or to one of the built-ins above.  |  Missing or empty filesystem tables keep filesystem access restricted and emit a startup warning.  |  extends = ":workspace"
facts.notes: Filesystem entries map paths/special tokens (:minimal, :workspace_roots, :tmpdir, :slash_tmp) to read/write/deny. The docs say 'deny' beats 'write' beats 'read' on the same path. Network is set per profile: [permissions.<name>.network] enabled = true.

facts.claim: Permission profiles compose with -s/--sandbox
facts.quote: Permission profiles do not compose with the older sandbox settings. Configure either `default_permissions` and `[permissions]`, or `sandbox_mode` / `sandbox_workspace_write`, but not both.
facts.notes: -s sets sandbox_mode, so do not combine -s or --approve-for-me (which sets sandbox_mode=workspace-write) with default_permissions. Which one wins if both are set is not documented.

facts.claim: codex exec has a CLI flag that selects a permission profile
facts.source: command: ssh sail-gpu 'codex sandbox --help' and 'codex exec --help'
facts.quote: (codex sandbox only) -P, --permission-profile <NAME>  Named permissions profile to apply from the active configuration stack
facts.notes: For exec, use -c default_permissions="<name>" or put it in a -p config layer. 'codex sandbox -P <name> -- <cmd>' can test a profile outside an agent run.

facts.claim: Per-domain network allowlists apply only when the managed network proxy is on
facts.quote: Domain rules for sandboxed commands. Enforced only when `features.network_proxy` or enabled administrator-managed networking requirements activate the proxy.  |  `unix_sockets` unset: No Unix socket destinations are allowed until you add explicit `allow` rules.
facts.notes: In proxy mode the Linux seccomp filter also denies socket(AF_UNIX) (codex-35), so proxy mode additionally blocks systemctl --user unless unix sockets are explicitly allowed.

facts.claim: --approve-for-me expands to approvals_reviewer=auto_review + approval_policy=on-request + sandbox_mode=workspace-write
facts.quote: --approve-for-me  Route approval requests through automatic review using the workspace-write sandbox  |  raw_overrides == [approvals_reviewer="auto_review", approval_policy="on-request", sandbox_mode="workspace-write"]
facts.notes: It has a hidden alias, --not-so-yolo. At the same level it conflicts with --sandbox, --ask-for-approval and --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox. A later 'exec --sandbox X' partially overrides it. The exec test asserts stderr contains 'approval: on-request' and 'sandbox: workspace-write'.

facts.claim: Auto-review requests are judged by a separate Codex reviewer agent. The default model is codex-auto-review (with ChatGPT auth; API-key auth uses gpt-5.6-luna)
facts.quote: itself a Codex agent with a narrower job than the main agent: decide whether a specific boundary-crossing action should run.  |  pub const DEFAULT_APPROVAL_REVIEW_PREFERRED_MODEL: &str = "codex-auto-review";  |  const API_KEY_APPROVAL_REVIEW_PREFERRED_MODEL: &str = "gpt-5.6-luna";
facts.notes: The docs page does not name the model. codex-auto-review appears in the server's models_cache.json. The source calls the reviewer 'guardian' (codex-rs/core/src/guardian).

facts.claim: Auto-review can approve sandbox escalations, blocked network requests, writes outside writable roots and MCP tool calls. It is told to deny exfiltration, credential probing, broad or persistent security weakening, and irreversible destructive actions
facts.quote: Shell or exec tool calls that request escalated sandbox permissions / Network requests blocked by the current sandbox or policy / File edits outside the allowed writable roots  |  sending private data, secrets, or credentials to untrusted destinations / probing for credentials, tokens, cookies, or session material / broad or persistent security weakening / destructive actions with significant risk of irreversible damage
facts.notes: Each decision is made per request by a model, so it is non-deterministic. Whether 'git push to GitHub' or 'install a systemd --user unit' gets approved is not documented. A local policy file can be supplied via auto_review.policy (a managed guardian_policy_config takes precedence).

facts.claim: Auto-review fails closed, times out after 90 s, and has a circuit breaker that interrupts the turn
facts.quote: 3. Fail closed on timeout, execution failure, or malformed output.  |  GUARDIAN_REVIEW_TIMEOUT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(90)  |  3 consecutive denials or 10 denials within a rolling window of the last 50 reviews in the same turn
facts.notes: When the breaker trips, the source returns GuardianRejectionCircuitBreakerAction::InterruptTurn, so the exec run ends mid-task. On a denial, the docs say: 'Codex returns the review rationale to the main agent and adds a stronger instruction: Do not pursue the same outcome via workaround, indirect execution, or policy circumvention.'

facts.claim: Auto-review does nothing with approval 'never' or with full access / yolo
facts.quote: Auto-review only applies when approvals are interactive  |  Full Access (`never` approvals with a disabled sandbox) approves without review.
facts.notes: The exec test exec_bypass_preserves_never_for_auto_review_config shows that --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox keeps 'approval: never' even when the config sets auto_review.

facts.claim: --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox (alias --yolo) removes both the sandbox and approvals, and also skips the git-repo check
facts.quote: Skip all confirmation prompts and execute commands without sandboxing. EXTREMELY DANGEROUS. Intended solely for running in environments that are externally sandboxed  |  Run every command without approvals or sandboxing. Only use inside an externally hardened environment.  |  // When --yolo (dangerously_bypass_approvals_and_sandbox) is set, also skip the git repo check
facts.notes: In source it sets SandboxMode::DangerFullAccess. It is the only built-in mode in which the GPU, the systemd user bus, .git writes and the network all work with no extra configuration.

facts.claim: -o/--output-last-message writes the agent's final message to a file
facts.quote: -o, --output-last-message <FILE>  Specifies file where the last message from the agent should be written
facts.notes: It is a global exec flag: it also works on 'exec resume' and 'exec fork'.

facts.claim: --json prints a JSONL event stream
facts.quote: --json  Print events to stdout as JSONL  |  event types include `thread.started`, `turn.started`, `turn.completed`, `turn.failed`, `item.*`, and `error`
facts.notes: It has an alias, --experimental-json. Capture the thread id from the thread.started event; it is the handle for 'codex exec resume <id>'.

facts.claim: --output-schema constrains the final response to a JSON Schema
facts.quote: --output-schema <FILE>  Path to a JSON Schema file describing the model's final response shape
facts.notes: Also available on 'exec resume' and 'exec fork'.

facts.claim: --ephemeral exists in 0.153.4 and disables session persistence
facts.quote: --ephemeral  Run without persisting session files to disk
facts.notes: An ephemeral run cannot be resumed later, and the source bails with 'Ephemeral forks require a prompt'. Do not use it for builder/worker runs that may need resume or audit.

facts.claim: -C sets the working root. --add-dir adds more writable roots
facts.quote: -C, --cd <DIR>  Tell the agent to use the specified directory as its working root  |  --add-dir <DIR>  Additional directories that should be writable alongside the primary workspace
facts.notes: The .git/.codex/.agents protection also applies inside every added writable root (codex-31).

facts.claim: exec refuses to run outside a Git repo unless --skip-git-repo-check (or yolo) is given
facts.quote: Codex requires commands to run inside a Git repository to prevent destructive changes.  |  Not inside a trusted directory and --skip-git-repo-check was not specified.

facts.claim: codex exec resume <id|name> [PROMPT] and --last exist. --last is filtered to the cwd unless --all is given
facts.quote: [SESSION_ID]  Conversation/session id (UUID) or thread name. UUIDs take precedence if it parses. If omitted, use --last to pick the most recent recorded session  |  --all  Show all sessions (disables cwd filtering)  |  Resume the most recent chat from the current working directory.
facts.notes: The resume options are: -c, --last, --all, --enable/--disable, -i, --strict-config, -m, --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox, --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust, --thread-source, --skip-git-repo-check, --ephemeral, --ignore-user-config, --ignore-rules, --output-schema, --json, -o. There is no -s, -C, --add-dir, --approve-for-me or -p.

facts.claim: A resumed exec run uses the approval and sandbox settings of the resume invocation, not the original session's
facts.quote:
approval_policy: Some(config.permissions.approval_policy.value().into()),
        approvals_reviewer: approvals_reviewer_override,
        sandbox: sandbox.flatten(),
facts.notes: Established by reading the source; not tested at runtime. Each resume must restate permissions with -c sandbox_mode=..., -c approval_policy=..., -c approvals_reviewer=..., or the bypass flag. Otherwise it falls back to config defaults (read-only sandbox + never).

facts.claim: codex exec fork <SESSION_ID> [PROMPT] exists
facts.quote: Fork a previous session by id into a new session  |  Usage: codex exec fork [OPTIONS] <SESSION_ID> [PROMPT]

facts.claim: --thread-source labels new or forked threads. The values are user, subagent, guardian_review, memory_consolidation, or any custom feature string. exec defaults to user
facts.source: command: ssh sail-gpu 'codex exec --help'; https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.153.4/codex-rs/protocol/src/protocol.rs (enum ThreadSource); codex-rs/exec/src/lib.rs
facts.quote: --thread-source <SOURCE>  Source classification for newly created or forked threads  |  ThreadSource::User => "user", ThreadSource::Subagent => "subagent", ThreadSource::GuardianReview => "guardian_review"  |  thread_source.map(Into::into).unwrap_or(ThreadSource::User)
facts.notes: This is separate from the session 'source' (exec), which is what Desktop and the TUI filter on. Issue #42083 shows threads with source=exec and thread_source=user staying hidden. Setting --thread-source does not make exec threads visible in the app.

facts.claim: --full-auto is deprecated
facts.quote: Deprecated compatibility flag. Prefer `--sandbox workspace-write`; Codex prints a warning when this flag is used.
facts.notes: The 0.153.4 exec --help does not list it.

facts.claim: Network is off by default in workspace-write. It is enabled with sandbox_workspace_write.network_access = true (CLI: -c sandbox_workspace_write.network_access=true)
facts.quote: Allow outbound network access inside the workspace-write sandbox.  |  By default, the agent runs with network access turned off.  |  [sandbox_workspace_write] / network_access = true
facts.notes: The permission-profile equivalent is [permissions.<name>.network] enabled = true. Do not mix the two forms (codex-10).

facts.claim: In workspace-write, <root>/.git (and .codex, .agents) stay read-only, so git add/commit/fetch/push cannot write .git from inside the sandbox
facts.quote: In the default `workspace-write` sandbox policy, writable roots still include protected paths: `<writable_root>/.git` is protected as read-only whether it appears as a directory or file.
facts.notes: Consequence for a builder: git commit and push must run outside the sandbox, via an escalation (auto-review), an execpolicy allow rule (codex-36), or no sandbox. That git commit fails in-sandbox is inferred; it was not run.

facts.claim: The Linux sandbox (bwrap + seccomp) mounts a minimal /dev, which hides /dev/nvidia*
facts.quote: Linux uses `bwrap` plus `seccomp` by default.  |  In bubblewrap (`bubblewrap.c`, `SETUP_MOUNT_DEV`), `--dev /dev` creates the standard minimal nodes: null, zero, full, random, urandom, and tty.
facts.notes: Even the full-filesystem bwrap path says 'Preserve nodev on the root bind while exposing only standard devices.' The GPU is reliably visible only when the sandbox is disabled (danger-full-access or yolo). The docs mention no GPU or device option.

facts.claim: openai/codex#19676 (workspace-write sandbox blocks GPU access, no /dev/nvidia* in the bwrap namespace) is still open
facts.source: command: gh issue view 19676 -R openai/codex --json state,title,updatedAt (https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/19676)
facts.quote: "state":"OPEN","title":"[bug] workspace-write sandbox blocks GPU access (no /dev/nvidia* in bwrap namespace)","updatedAt":"2026-07-21T15:14:33Z"
facts.notes: The reporter later commented: 'no, this hasn't been fixed - the issue is still open, there's no PR referencing it, and the sandbox code on main ... still has no GPU/device-passthrough handling.'

facts.claim: openai/codex#3141 (Allow GPU access inside sandbox) is still open. The community workarounds are fragile
facts.quote: "state":"OPEN","title":"Allow GPU access inside sandbox","updatedAt":"2026-06-10T19:46:57Z"  |  (maintainer) There are security concerns about giving access to the GPU from within the sandbox.  |  (user) After the latest update it causes a sandbox error to have the config I proposed earlier: [sandbox_workspace_write] writable_roots = [ "/dev/nvidia", "/dev/dri" ]
facts.notes: The writable_roots=["/dev"] workaround gives mixed results: others report CUDA error 304 even with /dev visible. Do not design on it.

facts.claim: With network disabled, the seccomp filter denies connect() for every socket family including AF_UNIX, so systemctl --user (the D-Bus/systemd user bus) cannot work from inside the sandbox. With network_access=true and no proxy, no network seccomp filter is installed
facts.quote: NetworkSeccompMode::Restricted => { deny_syscall(&mut rules, libc::SYS_connect); ... // For `socket` we allow AF_UNIX (arg0 == AF_UNIX) and deny everything else.  |  !network_sandbox_policy.is_enabled() || allow_network_for_proxy
facts.notes: Established by reading the source; not tested at runtime. Recommended probe (not run, since it is outside the allowed command list): 'codex sandbox -c sandbox_mode="workspace-write" -c sandbox_workspace_write.network_access=true -- systemctl --user status'. If systemctl --user works from the sandbox, then 'systemd-run --user' is a full sandbox escape: treat it as privileged.

facts.claim: Execpolicy .rules can allow specific command prefixes to run outside the sandbox without a prompt, or forbid them
facts.quote: "allow": Run the command outside the sandbox without prompting.  |  "forbidden": Block the request without prompting.  |  Codex scans `rules/` under every active config layer at startup, including Team Config locations and the user layer at `~/.codex/rules/`. Project-local rules under `<repo>/.codex/rules/` load only when the project `.codex/` layer is trusted.  |  // Bypass sandbox only when every parsed command segment is explicitly allowed by execpolicy.
facts.notes: Syntax: prefix_rule(pattern=[...], decision=..., justification=...). Whether forbidden rules are enforced under --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox is not documented; the source computes Forbidden regardless of sandbox mode, but this was not tested. 'exec --ignore-rules' disables all rules. Prefix matching can be evaded by reordering arguments (e.g. 'git push origin main --force'), so it is a guardrail, not a security boundary.

facts.claim: Rollouts are stored as JSONL under ~/.codex/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/, with thread state in SQLite (state_5.sqlite, thread_history_1.sqlite) plus session_index.jsonl
facts.quote: rollout-2026-09-15T14-01-16-<uuid>.jsonl ; state_5.sqlite ; thread_history_1.sqlite ; session_index.jsonl ; archived_sessions  |  sqlite_home: Directory where Codex stores the SQLite-backed state DB used by agent jobs and other resumable runtime state.
facts.notes: Non-ephemeral exec threads use paginated history (source: history_mode: (!config.ephemeral).then_some(ThreadHistoryMode::Paginated)). 'codex migrate-rollouts' migrates legacy sessions. No file contents were read.

facts.claim: exec sessions are resumable in the TUI but hidden from the picker unless --include-non-interactive is given
facts.quote: --include-non-interactive  Include non-interactive sessions in the resume picker and --last selection  |  Made `--include-non-interactive` include `exec` and `appServer` sessions, while continuing to exclude subagent and unknown sources.
facts.notes: By default the picker shows only cli and vscode sources ('thread/list treats omitted or empty sourceKinds as interactive-only (cli, vscode)').

facts.claim: Threads started with codex exec appear in the Codex Desktop app thread list
facts.quote: This is more than the known behavior where untouched `exec` sessions are intentionally not enumerated.  |  A persisted thread originally created by `codex exec` can be opened/resumed in Codex Desktop and used as an ordinary interactive chat, but it disappears from Desktop sidebar/search after navigating away.
facts.notes: Official docs say nothing either way. Issue evidence: exec threads are hidden in the Desktop sidebar by default and can only be opened by ID. Do not build a 'watch in the Codex app' feature on exec threads.

facts.claim: exec threads cannot be named from the CLI
facts.quote: `codex exec` creates a thread whose `name` is always NULL, and there is no supported way to set it from outside the interactive app.  |  Sessions created this way are also not written to `session_index.jsonl`, so `codex resume` does not list them.
facts.notes: Reported on codex-cli 0.155.1. Keep your own registry (thread id -> role/task) from the thread.started JSON event.

facts.claim: By default, environment variables whose names contain KEY/SECRET/TOKEN are passed through to the agent's commands
facts.quote: Keep variables containing KEY, SECRET, or TOKEN before other filters run (default: true). Set to false to apply automatic secret-name exclusions.
facts.notes: On a shared account this matters: VAST_API_KEY, GH_TOKEN, bot tokens etc. in the launcher environment reach the agent unless you set shell_environment_policy.ignore_default_excludes=false or filters. The Vast CLI key also sits in a file (~/.config/vastai/vast_api_key) that any unsandboxed agent can read.

facts.claim: Model slugs available to this account per ~/.codex/models_cache.json
facts.source: command: ssh sail-gpu python3 one-liner printing only the 'slug' field of each entry in ~/.codex/models_cache.json['models']
facts.quote:
gpt-6-astra
gpt-reserve
gpt-5.6-sol
gpt-5.6-terra
gpt-5.6-luna
gpt-5.5
codex-auto-review
facts.notes: codex-auto-review is the approval-reviewer model (codex-14), not a main-agent model. The configured default model was not read (config.toml was not opened).

facts.claim: vastai CLI 1.8.0 at ~/.local/bin/vastai on sail-gpu
facts.notes: Its help says: '--api-key API_KEY  API Key to use. defaults to using the one stored in /home/aurnab/.config/vastai/vast_api_key' (a shared-account key).

facts.claim: CPU fields are cpu_cores, cpu_cores_effective, cpu_ram, cpu_ghz and cpu_arch. There is no cpu_name query field, but cpu_name appears in --raw output
facts.source: command: ssh sail-gpu 'vastai search offers --help' + --raw key list
facts.quote: cpu_cores:              int       # virtual cpus  |  cpu_cores_effective:    float     # virtual cpus you get  |  cpu_ram:                float     system RAM in gigabytes  |  cpu_ghz:                Float     # cpu clock speed GHZ
facts.notes: Raw JSON keys include cpu_name, cpu_ram (observed in MB, e.g. 32.2 GB -> ~32200), dph_base, dph_total, storage_total_cost, discounted_dph_total, end_date, duration, reliability2 and verification. cpu_cores_effective is your share of a big host: e.g. a 256-core host sells 32 effective cores.

facts.claim: Cost fields are dph ($/h), inet_up_cost and inet_down_cost ($/GB), and storage_cost ($/GB/month). dph_total works for sorting and appears in raw output
facts.source: command: ssh sail-gpu 'vastai search offers --help' + query with -o 'dph_total'
facts.quote: dph:                    float     $/hour rental cost  |  inet_down_cost:         float     internet download bandwidth cost in $/GB  |  inet_up_cost:           float     internet upload bandwidth cost in $/GB  |  storage_cost:           float     storage cost in $/GB/month
facts.notes: dph_total is not in the documented query-field list, but -o 'dph_total' returned offers in ascending dph_total order. dph_total includes storage priced at --storage (default 5 GiB).

facts.claim: reliability, verified, rentable, disk_space and disk_bw are query fields
facts.quote: reliability:            float     machine reliability score (see FAQ for explanation)  |  verified:               bool      is the machine verified  |  rentable:               bool      is the instance currently rentable  |  disk_space:             float     disk storage space, in GB
facts.notes: The raw output has no 'verified' key; it has 'verification' (e.g. 'verified').

facts.claim: duration (max rental days) is a query field. end_date is only in raw output
facts.source: command: ssh sail-gpu 'vastai search offers --help' + --raw output
facts.quote: duration:               float     max rental duration in days
facts.notes: In raw output, duration is in seconds and end_date is epoch seconds; both were consistent in the snapshot. Some cheap offers expire within days (one 5090 had max_days 0.2), so filter e.g. 'duration>7' for long jobs.

facts.claim: Search supports on-demand, reserved and interruptible (bid) pricing, default on-demand. Interruptible instances are created with --bid_price
facts.source: command: ssh sail-gpu 'vastai search offers --help' and 'vastai create instance --help'
facts.quote: -t TYPE, --type TYPE     Show 'on-demand', 'reserved', or 'bid'(interruptible) pricing. default: on-demand  |  -i, --interruptible      Alias for --type=bid  |  --bid_price BID_PRICE             (OPTIONAL) create an INTERRUPTIBLE instance with per machine bid price in $/hour
facts.notes: Other aliases: -b (bid), -d (on-demand), -r (reserved). min_bid ($/hr) is a query field.

facts.claim: Sort with -o using a comma-separated field list. A '-' suffix sorts descending. The default is score-
facts.quote: -o ORDER, --order ORDER  Comma-separated list of fields to sort on. postfix field with - to sort desc. ex: -o 'num_gpus,total_flops-'.  default='score-'

facts.claim: Search adds a default filter and prices storage at 5 GiB by default. A call returned 64 offers
facts.source: command: ssh sail-gpu 'vastai search offers --help' + observed N_OFFERS_RETURNED=64
facts.quote: query                    Query to search for. default: 'external=false rentable=true verified=true', pass -n to ignore default  |  --storage STORAGE        Amount of storage to use for pricing, in GiB. default=5.0GiB
facts.notes: The 64-result cap is observed behaviour; use --limit for more.

facts.claim: Labels can be set at create time or later, and show instances can filter by label
facts.source: command: ssh sail-gpu 'vastai create instance --help', 'vastai label instance --help', 'vastai show instances --help'
facts.quote: --label LABEL                     label to set on the instance  |  usage: vastai label instance <id> <label>  |  --label LABEL [LABEL ...]                        filter by instance label; pass empty string '' for unlabeled
facts.notes: On the shared account, only ever touch instances whose label carries this project's prefix. 'show instances --label' makes that filter server-side.

facts.claim: Each instance gets a per-instance API key (CONTAINER_API_KEY) and its id (CONTAINER_ID), which allow self-stop and self-destroy from inside the container
facts.quote:
Each instance comes with a per-instance API key stored in the `CONTAINER_API_KEY` environment variable, allowing you to run CLI commands from within the container.  |  vastai stop instance $CONTAINER_ID
vastai destroy instance $CONTAINER_ID
facts.notes: The key's permission scope is not documented beyond the stop/destroy example. VAST_CONTAINERLABEL is described as 'Unique name/ID of your instance'.

facts.claim: The vastai CLI picks up CONTAINER_API_KEY automatically
facts.source: https://github.com/vast-ai/vast-cli (vastai/_base.py docstring, via gh code search 2026-09-23)
facts.quote: Resolves the API key from (in order): 1. Explicit argument 2. VAST_API_KEY environment variable 3. XDG config file: $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/vastai/vast_api_key ... 4. Legacy file: ~/.vast_api_key
facts.notes: CONTAINER_API_KEY is not in that resolution list (main branch; not verified against 1.8.0). Pass it explicitly: vastai --api-key "$CONTAINER_API_KEY" stop instance "$CONTAINER_ID".

facts.claim: A per-instance SSH key is attached with 'vastai attach ssh <instance_id> <ssh_key>'
facts.quote: usage: vastai attach ssh instance_id ssh_key  |  Attach an ssh key to an instance. This will allow you to connect to the instance with the ssh key.
facts.notes: Examples in the help accept a literal key, $(cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub), or a .pub path.

facts.claim: Data can be copied off a stopped instance (vastai copy between instances, and cloud sync)
facts.quote: The 3 built-in methods discussed here are unique in that they offer ways to copy data to/from a stopped instance, with some constraints.  |  Instances can be stopped/inactive. See complete Constraints below.  |  The Cloud Sync feature allows you to copy data to/from instance local storage and several cloud storage providers (S3, gdrive, backblaze, etc) - even when the instance is stopped.
facts.notes: Copy formats: [instance_id:]path, C.<id>:path, local:path, V.<volume>:path, <cloud>.<conn_id>:path. From the CLI help: 'You should not copy to /root or / as a destination directory'. The docs do not say explicitly that the C.<id>:path -> local:path form works on a stopped source.

facts.claim: Stopping keeps the data. Restarting depends on the machine being available
facts.quote: When an instance is "stopped" all of your data on the instance is preserved, and you can resume use of your instance by starting it again. Once stopped, starting an instance is subject to resource availability on the machine that the instance is located on.
facts.notes: Whether storage is billed while stopped was not verified in this pass.

facts.claim: IROS 2027 is in Florence, 26 Sep - 1 Oct 2027
facts.source: https://2027.ieee-iros.org/ (official site; iros2027.org does not resolve)
facts.quote: Human-Centric Robots for Sustainable Life 📅 September 26 – October 1, 2027 📍 Fortezza da Basso, Florence, Italy
facts.notes: The official landing page has no deadlines, CFP, page limits or template yet (/important-dates/ returns 404).

facts.claim: The IROS 2027 paper submission deadline is 2027-03-01
facts.quote: Mar 1, 2027 Paper submission deadline: IROS Submit your research papers and proposals for 2027 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS).
facts.notes: The source is the RAS calendar only; the official IROS 2027 site has no deadline yet. No time zone is given. A secondary aggregator (mldeadlines.com, search snippet only, not verified) says 23:59:59 America/Los_Angeles. For comparison, IROS 2026 was 'March 2, 2026 – Deadline for Paper submissions'.

facts.claim: An RA-L submission with the IROS option (and its own deadline) exists for 2027
facts.quote: IROS no longer offers an RA-L+IROS submission option. All published papers from RAM and non-evolutionary published RA-L, T-ASE and T-RO papers are eligible for presentation at IROS, during an eligibility time window.  |  Reminder: there are no conference-specific submission deadlines for RA-L papers.
facts.notes: The IROS 2026 CFP dropped the option. The 2027 CFP is not out, but the RA-L page lists a transfer window instead (venue-04).

facts.claim: An accepted RA-L paper can be presented at IROS 2027 within the transfer window
facts.quote: IROS 2027: August 1, 2026 to April 30, 2027  |  The paper must be transferred within 270 days of acceptance

Whether the dates refer to acceptance or transfer dates is paraphrased by the fetch tool; confirm before relying on edge dates.

facts.claim: IROS papers are 6+2 pages
facts.quote: Papers should be up to eight pages (US letter size) in length. The number of pages includes the references, appendices, etc. This replaces the old 6+2 model, and there is no option to pay for additional pages.
facts.notes: This is the IROS 2026 rule. The IROS 2027 page limit is not documented yet; assume 8 pages all-inclusive until the 2027 CFP appears.

facts.claim: RA-L letters are 6 pages plus up to 2 paid extra pages, with references counted
facts.quote: Letters will be six pages long in two-column IEEE format (see below for details), including figures and references, with up to two extra pages with extra page charges, for a maximum of eight pages.  |  These page limits include everything needed for publication, e.g., figures, tables, and any appendices.
facts.notes: The extra-page charge is $175 per page, as quoted in another fetch of the same page ('at most two extra pages allowed at a charge ($175 per extra page)').

facts.claim: T-RO regular papers: 18 pages at first submission, 20 pages maximum final, with a mandatory $175/page charge beyond 12. T-RO no longer takes new short papers
facts.quote: First submissions should be no more than 18 pages  |  Final Regular submissions may be a maximum of 20 pages long.  |  a mandatory page charge (see below) applies to each page beyond 12, up to a maximum of 20 pages  |  include everything needed for publication, e.g., figures, tables, references.
facts.notes: Communication items: max 4 pages, charged beyond 3. Surveys: max 20, charged beyond 14. The T-RO landing page steers shorter work (8 pages or fewer) to RA-L.

facts.claim: T-RO's scope covers rehabilitation and wearable robotics
facts.quote: medical robotics and computer-integrated surgery; rehabilitation and healthcare robotics
facts.notes: The word 'exoskeleton' was not seen in the scope text. The fetch tool also reported a 'Special Section on Wearable Robots' among T-RO special collections (not independently verified).

facts.claim: T-MRB page limits: Original 12, Short 4, Review 12, Position 8, with $175 per page over the limit
facts.quote: Original Articles are typically 12 pages (page limit)  |  Short Articles are typically 4 pages (page limit)  |  Authors are charged $175/page for the pages exceeding the page limit.
facts.notes: The template is the IEEE Transactions double-column style (IEEE Author Center). Whether references count is not stated.

facts.claim: T-MRB's scope statement mentions exoskeletons
facts.quote: The IEEE T-MRB publishes non-incremental results on innovative systems that support the prevention, diagnosis, or treatment of human diseases.  |  Main journal topics include: Surgical robotics, Rehabilitation and assistive robotics, Bionic prostheses, ...  |  devices for physical and cognitive rehabilitation
facts.notes: 'exoskeleton' and 'wearable' do not appear; exoskeleton work fits under 'Rehabilitation and assistive robotics'. The bar is 'non-incremental' and disease-oriented (prevention/diagnosis/treatment).

facts.claim: Science Robotics Research Articles are up to 8000 words
facts.source: https://www.science.org/content/page/scirobotics-instructions-research-articles (text from search-engine snippet; direct fetch returned HTTP 403)
facts.quote: Research Articles can be up to 8000 words long and can be enhanced with online materials.
facts.notes: Abstract length, figure limit and reference limit were not verified (page blocked to automated fetch). Submission is via the Science portal.

facts.claim: IROS uses the IEEEtran conference class
facts.quote: To ensure formatting compliance (e.g. margins, fonts and size), use the provided templates  |  \documentclass[letterpaper, 10 pt, conference]{ieeeconf}  |  \IEEEoverridecommandlockouts  |  \overrideIEEEmargins
facts.notes: IROS (PaperCept/PaperPlaza) supplies ieeeconf.cls in ieeeconf.zip (with root.tex), not IEEEtran.cls. US letter. The IROS 2027 template is not yet published; this is the 2026 CFP.

codex_exec_help:
Run Codex non-interactively
Usage: codex exec [OPTIONS] [PROMPT]
       codex exec [OPTIONS] <COMMAND> [ARGS]
Commands:
  resume  Resume a previous session by id or pick the most recent with --last
  fork    Fork a previous session by id into a new session
  review  Run a code review against the current repository
  help    Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)
Arguments:
  [PROMPT]
          Initial instructions for the agent. If not provided as an argument (or if `-` is used),
          instructions are read from stdin. If stdin is piped and a prompt is also provided, stdin
          is appended as a `<stdin>` block
Options:
  -c, --config <key=value>
          Override a configuration value that would otherwise be loaded from `~/.codex/config.toml`.
          Use a dotted path (`foo.bar.baz`) to override nested values. The `value` portion is parsed
          as TOML. If it fails to parse as TOML, the raw string is used as a literal.
          Examples: - `-c model="o3"` - `-c 'sandbox_permissions=["disk-full-read-access"]'` - `-c
          shell_environment_policy.inherit=all`
      --enable <FEATURE>
          Enable a feature (repeatable). Equivalent to `-c features.<name>=true`
      --disable <FEATURE>
          Disable a feature (repeatable). Equivalent to `-c features.<name>=false`
      --strict-config
          Error out when config.toml contains fields that are not recognized by this version of
          Codex
  -i, --image <FILE>...
          Optional image(s) to attach to the initial prompt
  -m, --model <MODEL>
          Model the agent should use
      --oss
          Use open-source provider
      --local-provider <OSS_PROVIDER>
          Specify which local provider to use (lmstudio or ollama). If not specified with --oss,
          will use config default or show selection
  -p, --profile <CONFIG_PROFILE_V2>
          Layer $CODEX_HOME/<name>.config.toml on top of the base user config
  -s, --sandbox <SANDBOX_MODE>
          Select the sandbox policy to use when executing model-generated shell commands
          [possible values: read-only, workspace-write, danger-full-access]
      --approve-for-me
          Route approval requests through automatic review using the workspace-write sandbox
      --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox
          Skip all confirmation prompts and execute commands without sandboxing. EXTREMELY
          DANGEROUS. Intended solely for running in environments that are externally sandboxed
      --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust
          Run enabled hooks without requiring persisted hook trust for this invocation. DANGEROUS.
          Intended only for automation that already vets hook sources
  -C, --cd <DIR>
          Tell the agent to use the specified directory as its working root
      --add-dir <DIR>
          Additional directories that should be writable alongside the primary workspace
      --thread-source <SOURCE>
          Source classification for newly created or forked threads
      --skip-git-repo-check
          Allow running Codex outside a Git repository
      --ephemeral
          Run without persisting session files to disk
      --ignore-user-config
          Do not load `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml`; auth still uses `CODEX_HOME`
      --ignore-rules
          Do not load user or project execpolicy `.rules` files
      --output-schema <FILE>
          Path to a JSON Schema file describing the model's final response shape
      --color <COLOR>
          Specifies color settings for use in the output
          [default: auto]
          [possible values: always, never, auto]
      --json
          Print events to stdout as JSONL
  -o, --output-last-message <FILE>
          Specifies file where the last message from the agent should be written
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
  -V, --version
          Print version

vast_offer_snapshot.method: Read-only 'vastai search offers ... -o dph_total --raw' on sail-gpu (vastai 1.8.0), piped to python3. No instance, rental or label commands were run. The CLI default query (external=false rentable=true verified=true) also applies. dph_total includes 5 GiB of storage (the --storage default). usd_per_eff_core_hr = dph_total / cpu_cores_effective. cpu_ram_gb = raw cpu_ram / 1000. max_days = raw duration / 86400.
vast_offer_snapshot.cpu_heavy_query: vastai search offers 'cpu_cores_effective>=32 num_gpus=1 verified=true rentable=true' -o 'dph_total' --raw  (64 offers returned; 15 cheapest shown; on-demand pricing)
vast_offer_snapshot.rtx5090_query: vastai search offers 'gpu_name=RTX_5090 verified=true rentable=true' -t on-demand -o 'dph_total' --raw  (64 offers returned; 10 cheapest shown; all 1x GPU; all verification=verified)
observations: Cheapest CPU per dollar in this snapshot: the RTX 5070 Ti host (EPYC 7V12, 128 effective cores, 515.6 GB RAM) at $0.3268/h = $0.00255 per effective core-hour. Next are V100/A16/T4 hosts at about $0.0033-0.0034. Old Xeon E5 v3/v4 cores are much slower per core, so rank by measured transitions/s per $, not by core count.
The cheapest on-demand verified RTX 5090 cost $0.468-0.60/h. Their CPU shares were 8-48 effective cores, and several expire within 1-8 days (max_days 0.2-8.0).
Bandwidth prices varied 500x ($0.0001-0.052/GB) and storage 9x ($0.067-0.6/GB/month). A cost model per transition must add storage (per GB-month) and inet_down (dataset/checkpoint pulls) to dph.

min_bid is below the on-demand price on most offers (e.g. 5090 id 49250870: $0.28 bid vs $0.468 on-demand). One raw record showed min_bid above dph_total (id 48989714), so do not assume bid < on-demand.

design_implications: BUILDER permission mode (must install packages, use the network, start GPU systemd --user units, push to GitHub): no sandboxed Codex 0.153.4 mode meets all four with no extra configuration. (a) The GPU is invisible in read-only/workspace-write (#19676 and #3141 open; bwrap mounts a minimal /dev). (b) .git is read-only in workspace-write, so commits and pushes fail in-sandbox. (c) With network off, seccomp denies connect(), so systemctl --user fails. (d) Network is off by default.

Safest mode that runs unattended and reliably: 'codex exec --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox' (the only mode where all four work), made safe by an external boundary. Use a dedicated Linux user for the builder with no sudo and no read access to the shared Vast key (~/.config/vastai) or other users' homes. Give it a repo-scoped GitHub credential (deploy key or fine-grained PAT for one repo) and server-side branch protection on main. Put resource caps (MemoryMax/CPUQuota/TasksMax) on its systemd --user slice and enable lingering. Strip secrets from the environment (shell_environment_policy.ignore_default_excludes=false; the default passes KEY/SECRET/TOKEN vars through). Add execpolicy 'forbidden' rules (git push --force, vastai create/destroy/stop, rm -rf of home) as a guardrail only: their enforcement under bypass is undocumented and prefix rules can be evaded.

More-contained alternative, if the user accepts occasional stalls: 'codex exec --approve-for-me -c sandbox_workspace_write.network_access=true --add-dir <caches>' plus execpolicy 'allow' rules for exact prefixes that must run unsandboxed (git add/commit/push origin <branch>; one vetted launcher such as ~/bin/forge-launch that writes and starts GPU units, kept outside the workspace and not writable by the agent). Everything else stays sandboxed, and other escalations go to the codex-auto-review reviewer. Costs: the reviewer is non-deterministic and fails closed after 90 s; 3 consecutive or 10 recent denials interrupt the turn. Do NOT allow bare 'systemd-run --user' or 'systemctl --user': either is an unrestricted sandbox escape.

Never mix the two permission systems. Use either sandbox_mode/sandbox_workspace_write (-s, --approve-for-me) or default_permissions/[permissions.<name>], not both. '-p/--profile' only layers $CODEX_HOME/<name>.config.toml (put builder/worker settings there). exec has no -P or -a flag, so use -c default_permissions=... and -c approval_policy=....

Headless default is approval 'never': a blocked command fails back to the model and never hangs. Only auto_review turns on-request prompts back on. The loop wrapper must treat turn.failed or an interrupted turn as 'resume with the same permission flags'. 'codex exec resume' does not remember the original permissions and has no -s, so restate them with -c or the bypass flag on every resume.

Session handling: never use --ephemeral for builder/worker runs. Record thread ids from the --json 'thread.started' event in your own registry (exec threads cannot be named, #46804). Use -o for the final message and --output-schema for structured results. Rollouts are in ~/.codex/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/*.jsonl, with state in state_5.sqlite. exec threads are hidden in the Codex Desktop sidebar (#42083 open) and in the TUI picker unless 'codex resume --include-non-interactive' is used, so the Watch/Steer panels should read the JSONL/rollouts rather than rely on the Codex app. exec needs a git repo or --skip-git-repo-check.

GPU work should always run as systemd --user units, outside the Codex sandbox, launched by a vetted launcher. Do not rely on the writable_roots=['/dev'] workaround: results are mixed and one report says it now errors.

Vast 'transitions per dollar' policy: rank offers by measured env-steps/s divided by (dph_total + storage GB x storage_cost/730 + expected GB x inet_down_cost), not by cpu_cores_effective. Filter on duration (max_days) against job length and on reliability, and sort with -o 'dph_total'. In this snapshot, CPU-heavy hosts started at about $0.0026 per effective core-hour and 1x RTX 5090 at $0.468/h (8-48 effective cores).

Vast shared-account safety: label every instance at create time (--label <project-prefix>) and only ever list or act on instances via 'vastai show instances --label <prefix>'. For in-container self-stop use 'vastai --api-key "$CONTAINER_API_KEY" stop instance "$CONTAINER_ID"' (the CLI key lookup does not document CONTAINER_API_KEY). Stopped instances keep their data and can be copied out with vastai copy or cloud sync; do not copy to / or /root.

Venues: IROS 2027 (Florence, 26 Sep-1 Oct 2027) has a paper deadline of 2027-03-01 per the RAS calendar only; re-check the official CFP for the time zone, page limit (2026 was 8 pages all-inclusive, no paid extras) and template (ieeeconf.cls, not IEEEtran). There is no RA-L+IROS option: an RA-L paper accepted between 2026-08-01 and 2027-04-30 can be transferred to IROS 2027. For exoskeleton work, BioRob 2027 (RA-L window to 2027-04-01) and T-MRB (12 pages, disease/rehabilitation framing) fit. T-RO allows up to 20 pages, charged beyond 12.

Version drift: the server runs codex-cli 0.153.4 while 0.155.1 is already in the wild. Pin the version for the programme, and re-run 'codex exec --help' plus these source checks before relying on flags after any upgrade.
